outcomes.text: Explain how pitch is organised melodically and harmonically, including harmonic change and cadences such as the interrupted cadence.
Recognise complex chord progressions such as secondary dominants, and melodic devices such as augmentation.
Explain how keys relate through the circle of fifths, and complex or remote key relationships such as enharmonic change.
Describe complex structures such as sonata form, fugue and through-composed music.
Describe combinations of vocal timbres and instrumental techniques such as con sordino and sul ponticello.
Identify textures such as homophony, polyphony and fugue.
Describe metrical and rhythmic devices: changing metres, syncopation, additive rhythm and polyrhythm.
Describe expressive use of dynamics, including contrast, extended ranges and refined control.
Explain how the purpose and intention of composer, performer or commissioner shape how music is created and performed.
Explain how audience, time and place shape music across historical, social and cultural contexts.
Describe how music from different contexts has changed over time.
Read and write staff notation, including compound time, irregular time signatures and all key signatures.
Use chords and chord symbols, including inversions, dominant 7ths and extended chords such as secondary 7ths and 9ths.
Recognise and use musical terms for the areas of study, such as glissando, conjunct and portamento.
Use sophisticated terminology to describe music accurately.

topics.title: Area of Study 1: Instrumental Music of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven

outcomes.text: Analyse, evaluate and judge Classical chamber music, symphony, concerto and sonata using listening and context.
Study the prescribed work in depth alongside the music around it.
Compare developments in Classical instrumental style, its characteristics and principles.
Explain the forms and style of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven.
Describe the Classical orchestra, instrumental techniques and articulation.
Explain melodic construction, phrasing and structure.
Explain harmonic language: inversions, cadences and progressions.
Explain instrumentation, texture, dynamics and expressive devices.
Explain the historical and social context of Classical music.
Explain how purpose and intention shaped the music and the working conditions of musicians.
Read and write the associated staff notation.

topics.title: Area of Study 2: Popular Song: Blues, Jazz, Swing and Big Band

outcomes.text: Analyse and evaluate vocal jazz and blues, popular solo song, vocal artists' recordings and interpretation of standards.
Study the prescribed work in depth within its wider context.
Compare song structures in styles of jazz.
Describe performing techniques such as improvisation.
Explain the delivery and expression of lyrics and the treatment of melody and words.
Describe vocal techniques: belt, register, articulation and vibrato.
Explain accompaniment and the relationship of voice and accompaniment.
Explain dynamics and expressive devices, and how pitch is organised.
Explain how audience, time, place and recording technology shaped the songs.
Explain the historical and social context of the songs and musicians' working conditions.

topics.title: Area of Study 3: Developments in Instrumental Jazz 1910 to the present day

outcomes.text: Study recorded jazz performances in depth using recordings, live performance and scores.
Analyse and judge jazz with technical vocabulary.
Compare early jazz, swing, bebop and cool jazz.
Compare hard bop, avant-garde and free jazz, jazz-rock fusion and contemporary approaches.
Explain improvisation, swing, syncopation and polyrhythm.
Explain harmony, tonality, blues, blue notes and note decoration.
Explain timbre, call and response, riff, ostinato and chorus devices.
Describe roles of solo, ensemble and rhythm section.
Describe the origins of jazz in New Orleans and its spread across the USA and Europe.
Explain changes in popularity and commercial viability, and the roles of radio and recording.
Describe jazz musicians' working conditions and today's challenges.

topics.title: Area of Study 4: Religious Music of the Baroque Period

outcomes.text: Study sacred Baroque vocal music in depth through recordings, performances and scores.
Analyse and judge it using technical vocabulary.
Compare Italian Catholic traditions: Venetian concertato, a cappella style and oratorio.
Compare Lutheran and Catholic German music: chorale, passion, church cantata.
Compare Anglican motet and English oratorio, and French grand motet, petit motet and cantata.
Explain harmony and tonality, and structures such as recitative, aria and chorus.
Explain textures: chordal, fugal, imitative, solo and choral.
Explain word setting, resources, obbligato accompaniment, and rhythm from dance patterns.
Explain worship, liturgy and the opportunities and limits they placed on music.
Describe how music spread through publishing.
Describe church musicians' working conditions and training at centres such as St Mark's Venice and St Thomas's Leipzig.
Study Romantic orchestral, chamber and solo programme music in depth.
Analyse and judge it using technical vocabulary.
Compare concert overture, symphonic poem and programme symphony.
Compare solo works and works expressing national identity.
Explain expressive harmony, dissonance and modulation.
Explain how structure and expressive freedom combine, including adapted sonata form.
Explain expanded orchestras, piano improvements, virtuoso soloists and the conductor.
Explain developments in dynamics, articulation, texture and dramatic contrast.
Explain the Romantic movement in the arts and the influence of opera on concert music.
Explain technological advances such as valved brass and piano making.
Explain audience change, public concerts, orchestras, and transmission of music across Europe and the USA.
Describe musicians' working conditions.

topics.title: Area of Study 6: Innovations in Music 1900 to the present day

outcomes.text: Study Western music from 1900 to today in depth through recordings, performances and scores.
Analyse and judge it using technical vocabulary.
Compare late Romantic style, impressionism, and expressionism with atonality and serialism.
Compare neo-classicism and folk-based national styles.
Compare post-1945 avant-garde, electronic and experimental music, minimalism and contemporary composition.
Explain irregular rhythm, metre, polyrhythm, polymetre and organisation of time.
Explain pitch, dissonance, harmony, modality and atonality.
Explain sonority, timbre, texture, percussion and technology.
Explain dynamics, extreme range, structure, notation, improvisation and aleatoric methods.
Explain audience reactions to innovation and the effect of technology and mass media.
Explain composers' responses to revolution, war, persecution and censorship.
Explain ideas about music's function: Gebrauchsmusik, popular crossover, film music and propaganda.
Describe working conditions and today's challenges for performers and composers.
Perform at least two contrasting pieces as solo, ensemble, accompanist or music-technology realisation.
Link the recital, if wished, to an Area of Study to inform performance choices.
Interpret and communicate musical ideas with technical and expressive control and an understanding of style and context.
Perform with control, continuity and suitable tempi, showing critical understanding of the music.
Perform fluently with a sense of the shape, direction and style of the music.
Perform with accuracy, fluency and technical control across a range of techniques.
Realise performance markings and conventions to interpret and communicate the music.
Practise varied pieces that build skill as soloist, ensemble member, accompanist or technology realiser.
Perform at least two contrasting pieces by playing, singing, ensemble work, improvising or music technology.
Interpret music with technical and expressive control and an understanding of style and context.
Perform with control, continuity, fluency and a sense of overall shape and style.
Perform accurately with technical control and realise performance markings and conventions.
Perform at least one further piece showing in-depth understanding of repertoire idiomatic to the chosen instrument.
Make informed musical choices showing the styles and techniques of idiomatic repertoire.

topics.title: Section 1: Composition to an OCR brief

outcomes.text: Create and develop musical ideas with technical control and expressive understanding in response to a brief from others.
Develop ideas showing understanding of the devices and conventions of the chosen genre, style and tradition.
Compose music that is convincing and uses musical elements in combination with sophistication.

topics.title: Section 2: Composition to a learner brief

outcomes.text: Compose freely, writing own brief to show ability to create and develop musical ideas.
Show understanding of devices and conventions of the chosen genre, style and tradition.
Make creative use of ideas that are musically convincing.
Compose short exercises that develop ideas using devices and conventions of a genre, style and tradition.
Show imaginative command of techniques within the chosen option, integrating ideas and technique.
Show control of ideas and technical knowledge of the chosen medium.

topics.title: Section 1: Composition to an OCR brief

outcomes.text: Create and develop ideas with technical control and expressive understanding in response to a brief or commission.
Develop ideas showing understanding of devices and conventions of the chosen genre, style and tradition.
Compose music that is convincing and uses musical elements in combination with sophistication.

topics.title: Section 2: Composition to a learner brief

outcomes.text: Compose freely, writing own brief to show ability to create and develop musical ideas.
Show understanding of devices and conventions of the chosen genre, style and tradition.
Make creative use of ideas that are musically convincing.
Analyse and evaluate music in aural and written form using knowledge of elements, contexts and language.
Make critical judgements about repertoire in the Areas of Study and about musical interpretations.
Judge unfamiliar music not named in the specification.
Form critical judgements through attentive listening, analysis, evaluation, contextualisation and reflection.
Comment in detail on music heard across the genres, styles and traditions studied.
Use acute aural perception and discrimination.
Show understanding of how musical elements depend on each other, and how music connects to its context.
